solution.concept_anchor: Privacy — three-fold test for restriction under Puttaswamy
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know that both A and R are accurate statements about the Puttaswamy judgment may assume the three-fold test directly explains why privacy is a fundamental right, when in fact the test explains when privacy can be restricted — a subtle logical inversion.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) unanimously held privacy to be a fundamental right under Article 21, overruling M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — the three-fold test (legality, legitimate aim, proportionality) is accurately stated; it is the standard for restricting privacy.

Step 3: Does R explain A? No — R describes the conditions under which privacy can be restricted, not the basis for holding it to be a fundamental right. The reason why privacy is an FR is that it is intrinsic to individual autonomy and dignity under Article 21 — R is a consequence (restriction framework) not a cause (basis for holding it an FR).
Both correct but R does NOT explain A → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap here inverts the logical sequence. R (the three-fold test) is invoked only after privacy is recognised as a fundamental right — it governs when the right can be restricted, not why it is a right. A student who knows both facts — that Puttaswamy upheld privacy and that the three-fold test exists — may assume R explains A without analysing the directional logic.
solution.final_explanation:
The K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) judgment has two distinct components: the holding that privacy is an FR, and the test for when that FR can be restricted.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The 9-judge bench in K.S. Puttaswamy unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 — intrinsic to human dignity and autonomy. This overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962).

Reason (R) — Correct: The three-fold test for restricting privacy — (i) legality (existence of a law), (ii) legitimate State aim, (iii) proportionality between means and aim — is accurately described in R.

Causal relationship — R does NOT explain A: R describes the framework for restricting privacy once it is recognised as an FR. It does not explain why or on what basis the Court held privacy to be an FR. The basis was the intrinsic connection between privacy, dignity, and liberty under Article 21 — not a restriction test. R is a post-recognition framework, not the rationale for recognition.

Value Addition:
• Puttaswamy (2017) is the longest Indian Supreme Court judgment — running over 500 pages with six separate concurring opinions.
• The three-fold test mirrors the ECtHR (European Court of Human Rights) proportionality framework.
• The judgment has been cited in subsequent cases involving Aadhaar data, marital rape, and LGBTQ rights (Navtej Johar, 2018).

solution.concept_anchor: S.P. Gupta — right to know derived from Articles 19(1)(a) and 21
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because the RTI Act (2005) is the most publicly known instrument of the right to information, and students may assume it was the first legal recognition rather than a statute that followed decades of judicial recognition.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Reliance Petrochemicals (1988) discussed the right to know but was not the founding case — S.P. Gupta (1981) preceded it; eliminate.
Confirm (b): S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) is the foundational case deriving the right to know from Articles 19(1)(a) and 21 — it predates the RTI Act by 24 years.
Eliminate (c): RTI Act (2005) is the statutory recognition, not the judicial source — it came after decades of judicial evolution.
Eliminate (d): Bennett Coleman (1972) dealt with newsprint policy and press freedom under Art. 19(1)(a) — not the right to know about government functioning.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes RTI Act (2005) for S.P. Gupta (1981) as the primary source of the right to information. Students who associate the right to information with the RTI Act may not recall the earlier judicial derivation. Option (a) uses Reliance Petrochemicals (1988), which is a secondary case that followed S.P. Gupta — a student who has heard of both cases may select the wrong one.
solution.final_explanation:
The right to information in India has a judicial lineage predating the RTI Act by over two decades.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Reliance Petrochemicals Ltd. v. Proprietors of Indian Express (1988) discussed the right to know but was not the foundational case — it built on S.P. Gupta.
• Option (b) — Correct: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), also known as the First Judges' Transfer Case, was the landmark judgment where the Supreme Court derived the right to know about government functioning from Articles 19(1)(a) and 21. The Court held that an open society requires informed citizens, making access to information a component of the right to free speech and the right to life.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The RTI Act (2005) is the statutory recognition of the judicially-evolved right — it came 24 years after S.P. Gupta. Statutes cannot be the 'first recognition' of judicial rights.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1972) addressed newsprint allocation policy and press freedom under Article 19(1)(a) — not the right to access government information.

Value Addition:
• The RTI Act has 10+ exemptions under Sections 8 and 9 — including intelligence agencies, security matters, and personal information.
• The Central Information Commission (CIC) adjudicates RTI disputes at the national level.
• The right to know and the right to privacy can conflict — Puttaswamy (2017) provides the proportionality framework for resolving such conflicts.

solution.concept_anchor: Post-44th Amendment — only Art. 20 and 21 non-suspendable

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978), all Fundamental Rights in Part III are equally immune from suspension during a National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment protected only Articles 20 and 21 from suspension during Emergency. Other Fundamental Rights, particularly Article 19 rights, can still be suspended under Article 358, and enforcement of other rights can be suspended under Article 359. The immunity is specific to Articles 20 and 21, not universal.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court's majority decision in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) has never been formally overruled, and remains technically good law in Indian constitutional jurisprudence.
statement_analysis.reason: ADM Jabalpur was expressly overruled by the Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), where Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (writing for himself) explicitly declared it wrongly decided. The decision has been formally negated.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because a student who correctly knows both statements deal with Emergency-era issues and are both likely incorrect might overcorrect and select 'Neither 1 nor 2' (i.e., both are correct), misreading the question as asking which are correct.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: The 44th Amendment made only Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable — not all Fundamental Rights; the qualifier 'all Fundamental Rights...equally immune' is false; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Test Statement 2: ADM Jabalpur was explicitly overruled in Puttaswamy (2017) by Justice Chandrachud — 'never been formally overruled' is false; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Both statements are NOT correct — answer is (a) Both 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses scope-extension by universalising the 44th Amendment's protection to 'all Fundamental Rights' when it applies only to Articles 20 and 21. A student who knows the 44th Amendment significantly strengthened fundamental rights may accept this overbroad statement. Statement 2 exploits the fact that many students are unaware that Puttaswamy (2017) formally overruled ADM Jabalpur — especially since that overruling occurred within a privacy case, not an Emergency case.
solution.final_explanation:
Emergency and fundamental rights is a topic where precision about which rights survive is critical.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 44th Amendment amended Article 359 to carve out only Articles 20 and 21 as non-suspendable during Emergency. Article 19 rights are automatically suspended under Article 358 when an External Emergency is proclaimed. Other rights can have their enforcement suspended under Article 359. The protection is specific, not universal.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: ADM Jabalpur was formally and expressly overruled by the Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). Justice D.Y. Chandrachud's concurrence explicitly held that the majority opinion in ADM Jabalpur was wrongly decided and is no longer good law.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 (automatic suspension of Art. 19 during External Emergency) vs. Article 359 (President may suspend enforcement of other FRs during any Emergency) — a commonly confused distinction.
• Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent in ADM Jabalpur is now canonically celebrated as the correct constitutional position.
• The 44th Amendment (Janata government) was specifically designed to undo the excesses exposed during the 1975–77 Internal Emergency.

solution.concept_anchor: Reputation as Article 21 right — Umesh Kumar (2013)
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) incorrectly pairs Subramanian Swamy with the first recognition of reputation as an Article 21 right — students who know Subramanian Swamy is the defamation case may conflate it with being the foundational reputation-as-FR case.
elimination_logic: Identify the case that first held reputation is part of Article 21: Umesh Kumar v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2013) — not Subramanian Swamy (2016).
Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation by applying the already-established principle from Umesh Kumar — it is not the foundational case.
Gian Kaur (1996) deals with right to die, not reputation — eliminate any option pairing Gian Kaur with reputation.
Option (c) correctly pairs Umesh Kumar (2013) with 'first recognition of reputation as a component of Article 21' — this is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces Umesh Kumar (2013) with Subramanian Swamy (2016) in the 'reputation as FR' pairing. Students who know the Subramanian Swamy case as the prominent defamation case may attribute the foundational reputation-as-FR holding to it, without knowing that Subramanian Swamy applied the principle rather than establishing it. The distinction between 'established principle' (Umesh Kumar) and 'applied principle' (Subramanian Swamy) is precisely the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The right to reputation as an Article 21 component has a clear foundational case.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: P. Rathinam (1994) dealt with the right to die and Section 309 IPC — unrelated to reputation as an Article 21 right.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) upheld the constitutional validity of criminal defamation — it applied the principle that reputation is an Article 21 right but did not first establish this principle. The foundational case was Umesh Kumar (2013).
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Umesh Kumar v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2013) is the case that first explicitly held that the right to reputation is an integral component of the right to life and dignity under Article 21.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) dealt with the broader right to live with dignity and basic necessities — it is not specifically about reputation.

Value Addition:
• The tension between Art. 19(1)(a) (free speech) and Art. 21 (reputation) is tested through the 'balancing test' — neither right is absolute.
• Criminal defamation (Sections 499/500 IPC) survives because protecting reputation = protecting an Article 21 right, which is a legitimate restriction on free speech under Article 19(2).
• Civil defamation under the Law of Torts remains separately available alongside the criminal remedy.

solution.concept_anchor: Maneka Gandhi — golden triangle is judge-made, Gopalan overruled

statement_analysis.statement: In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court held that fundamental rights in Part III operate independently as separate self-contained codes, and a law valid under one article cannot be challenged under another.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the 'specific entry' or 'watertight compartments' theory of Gopalan — the Court held that Part III articles are mutually exclusive, so the validity of the Preventive Detention Act was to be tested only under Article 22, not Articles 19 or 21.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'golden triangle' doctrine articulated in Maneka Gandhi (1978) is explicitly inscribed in the text of Part III of the Constitution as an interpretive principle for fundamental rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The golden triangle is entirely a judicial doctrine — it appears nowhere in the constitutional text. It was propounded by the Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi (1978) as an interpretive principle and has no separate constitutional provision.

statement_analysis.statement: After Maneka Gandhi (1978), a law that deprives a person of personal liberty must satisfy the requirements of Articles 14, 19, and 21 simultaneously, and failure under any one of these renders the law unconstitutional.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise holding of Maneka Gandhi — the golden triangle requires concurrent satisfaction of Article 14 (non-arbitrary), Article 19 (not unreasonably restricting freedoms), and Article 21 (fair, just, and reasonable procedure). Failure at any vertex is fatal to the law.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor for students who know both Statements 1 and 3 as historically accurate but have not studied whether the golden triangle is textual or judicial — leading them to assume Statement 2 is also correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: A.K. Gopalan (1950) — watertight compartments theory — correctly described; Statement 1 is correct.
Test Statement 2's claim 'explicitly inscribed in constitutional text': The golden triangle appears in no Part III article; it is pure judicial construction from Maneka Gandhi; Statement 2 is false.
Verify Statement 3: Post-Maneka Gandhi — law must satisfy Articles 14, 19, 21 simultaneously — this is the exact golden triangle test; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses partial-truth by taking the real concept (golden triangle exists) and adding a false attribute (inscribed in constitutional text). The golden triangle is among the most important judge-made doctrines in Indian constitutional law — its absence from the constitutional text is a critical distinction that tests whether students know the doctrine's source. The fact that Maneka Gandhi is a Supreme Court case, not a constitutional amendment, is the key differentiator.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gopalan–Maneka Gandhi shift represents the most important evolution in the methodology of fundamental rights adjudication.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A.K. Gopalan (1950) held that Part III articles are separate codes — a law is to be tested only against the article that specifically governs it. This meant the Preventive Detention Act could not be tested under Article 19 or 21 if Article 22 was satisfied. This theory was dismantled by Maneka Gandhi.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The golden triangle doctrine is entirely judge-made — propounded in Maneka Gandhi (1978) through judicial interpretation. It is not present in any Part III text or any constitutional amendment. This is a recurring UPSC-style trap.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Maneka Gandhi established that any law curtailing personal liberty must simultaneously satisfy: Article 14 (non-arbitrary), Article 19 (not unreasonably restricting listed freedoms), and Article 21 (fair, just, reasonable procedure). Failure at any point makes the law unconstitutional.

Value Addition:
• The Constituent Assembly's deliberate rejection of 'due process' (proposed by B.R. Ambedkar himself initially before opposition) was effectively bridged by Maneka Gandhi's reading.
• Bank Nationalisation Case (1970) and Rustom Cavasji Cooper (1970) had already begun to erode the Gopalan compartmentalisation before Maneka Gandhi's decisive overruling.
• Maneka Gandhi also established that 'law' in Article 21 must be a valid, enacted piece of legislation — executive orders alone are insufficient.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 47 non-justiciable but health enforced via Article 21
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually true, and students may reflexively assume R explains A since health being a DPSP and an FR sounds like a causal pair — missing that the DPSP status of Article 47 is not the reason health is justiciable under Article 21.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — through cases like Paschim Banga (1996), the right to health has become justiciable under Article 21 even though Article 47 itself is a non-justiciable DPSP.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — Article 47 is a Directive Principle under Part IV and is explicitly non-justiciable under Article 37; this is a correct statement of constitutional law.

Step 3: Does R explain A? No — R (Article 47 being non-justiciable) is the problem that judicial interpretation had to overcome, not the explanation of why health became justiciable. The reason health is justiciable is that courts read it into Article 21 (not because of Article 47 being a DPSP). R is a contrasting fact, not a causal explanation of A.
Both correct but R does NOT explain A → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap presents R as appearing to explain A through surface association (both discuss health). However, R (Article 47 is a non-justiciable DPSP) is actually the obstacle that the Court overcame — it is not the mechanism through which health became justiciable. The correct explanation of A is that courts derived the right to health from Article 21's expanded scope — the DPSP status of Article 47 is background context, not causation.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between non-justiciable DPSPs and enforceable fundamental rights is a nuanced area requiring precision.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The right to health and emergency medical care has been made justiciable by the Supreme Court through Article 21 — most prominently in Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) and Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995). Despite Article 47 being a DPSP, the substance of health protection is enforced as an Article 21 right.

Reason (R) — Correct: Article 47 is a Directive Principle under Part IV. Article 37 explicitly states that DPSPs 'shall not be enforceable by any court.' Article 47 is therefore non-justiciable on its own — a correct statement.

Causal relationship — R does NOT explain A: R describes the limitation of Article 47, which is the very limitation that courts sought to overcome. The reason health became justiciable under Article 21 is that the Supreme Court read the right to health into the expanded scope of Article 21 — not because Article 47 is a DPSP. R is background context that creates the problem; A describes the solution. R does not explain A.

Value Addition:
• This DPSP-via-Article 21 bridge applies to: Article 39A (free legal aid), Article 47 (health), Article 48A (environment), and Article 45 (early childhood care).
• The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A specifically to avoid reliance on this judicial bridge for the right to education.
• State liability for inadequate emergency health infrastructure was the core holding in Paschim Banga — a positive obligation on the State.

solution.concept_anchor: Francis Coralie Mullin and socio-economic rights expansion under Article 21

statement_analysis.statement: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Union Territory of Delhi (1981) was the first case in which the Supreme Court explicitly held that the right to life under Article 21 encompasses the right to live with human dignity, including access to basic necessities.
statement_analysis.reason: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) is precisely the foundational case for the 'right to live with dignity' doctrine — it expanded Article 21 beyond mere physical survival to include the minimum conditions of dignified existence, including food, clothing, and shelter.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court has interpreted Article 21 to include the right to food through the PUCL v. Union of India case (2001 onwards), making it a textually explicit fundamental right in the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The right to food derived from Article 21 through PUCL is a judicially-evolved right — it is not 'textually explicit' in the Constitution. The text of Article 21 does not mention food; the right was judicially read into it.

statement_analysis.statement: The judicial expansion of Article 21 to include livelihood, health, and shelter makes these rights fully absolute, placing them beyond any State restriction.
statement_analysis.reason: None of the socio-economic rights derived from Article 21 — livelihood, health, or shelter — are absolute. All are subject to restriction through fair, just, and reasonable procedure as established in the Maneka Gandhi framework. The State can restrict these rights for legitimate purposes.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Food Security Act, 2013 provides a statutory framework that operationalises the right to food — a right judicially derived from Article 21 through the PUCL litigation.
statement_analysis.reason: While the NFSA is an independent legislative enactment, it operationalises the food security framework that was the subject of the PUCL litigation. The Act provides statutory backing to what the courts were enforcing as an Article 21 obligation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor for students who accept Statement 2 as true because 'PUCL judicially evolved the right to food' — they may miss the specific false qualifier 'textually explicit' and count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 2: 'textually explicit fundamental right' — Article 21 text has no mention of food; PUCL derived it judicially; Statement 2 is false due to the 'textually explicit' qualifier.

Test Statement 3: 'fully absolute, beyond State restriction' — no Article 21 right (including derived ones) is absolute; Olga Tellis and Maneka Gandhi both confirm they can be restricted by fair procedure; Statement 3 is false.
Verify Statements 1 and 4: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) and NFSA (2013) as statutory operationalisation — both correctly described; both are correct.
Two correct statements (1 and 4) → answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 and Statement 3 both use the partial-truth technique. Statement 2 is partially correct (PUCL did derive a food right from Article 21) but adds the false qualifier 'textually explicit.' Statement 3 is partially correct (Article 21 covers these rights) but incorrectly characterises them as 'fully absolute.' Both traps target students who know the general correct concept but do not scrutinise the qualifying language.
solution.final_explanation:
The expansion of Article 21 to socio-economic rights has clear limits — none of these rights are textually enumerated or absolute.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) is the foundational case establishing that Article 21 means more than bare survival — it includes the right to live with human dignity, encompassing basic necessities. This was the philosophical starting point for all subsequent socio-economic expansions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The right to food is judicially derived, not textually enumerated. Article 21 says nothing about food. The PUCL litigation (2001 onwards) read the right to food into Article 21 through judicial interpretation — it is an implied, judge-made right.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Derived rights under Article 21 — livelihood (Olga Tellis), shelter (Chameli Singh), health (Paschim Banga) — are all subject to reasonable restrictions through fair, just, and reasonable procedure. No Article 21 right is absolute; they can be restricted for legitimate public purposes with procedural safeguards.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The National Food Security Act, 2013 provides the statutory framework for food entitlements, operationalising what PUCL orders had been enforcing as an Article 21 obligation — mid-day meals, PDS, ICDS benefits are all structured under this Act.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'textually enumerated' and 'judicially derived' rights is a major UPSC theme — only Article 21A (education) among socio-economic rights is textually inserted.
• The PUCL food case orders are among the longest-running PIL orders in Supreme Court history.
• Socio-economic rights in Article 21 are sometimes called 'second generation' human rights — distinct from the 'first generation' civil-political rights in Part III.

solution.concept_anchor: Vishaka and horizontal application — Article 21 vs. private actors

statement_analysis.statement: Article 21 of the Constitution is directly enforceable only against the 'State' as defined in Article 12, and courts have never extended any form of Article 21 obligations to private entities or individuals.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts have extended Article 21 obligations indirectly to private actors in specific contexts: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) imposed binding guidelines on private employers regarding sexual harassment; MC Mehta cases held private industries liable for environmental violations through absolute liability — these are indirect horizontal extensions.

statement_analysis.statement: In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court held that sexual harassment at the workplace by private employers constitutes a violation of Article 21 and issued binding guidelines on all employers, public and private, until Parliament enacted a law.
statement_analysis.reason: Vishaka (1997) is the landmark case on horizontal application — the Court held workplace sexual harassment violates Articles 14, 19, and 21, and issued comprehensive guidelines binding on all employers (public and private) pending legislative action. The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 subsequently codified these guidelines.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 2 is correct about Vishaka may then incorrectly also accept Statement 1 by reasoning that Article 21 still cannot be directly enforced against private parties (missing the word 'never' and the indirect extension).
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1's qualifier 'never extended any form of Article 21 obligations to private entities': Vishaka (1997) and MC Mehta cases directly contradict this — courts have extended obligations to private employers and industries; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Verify Statement 2: Vishaka (1997) — binding on all employers public and private — correctly described; Statement 2 IS correct.
Statement 1 is NOT correct, Statement 2 IS correct → the question asks which is NOT correct → answer is (a) 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses scope-extension by adding 'never' — transforming a technically accurate general rule (Article 21 is primarily vertical) into an absolute false claim (courts have 'never' extended obligations to private actors). Students who have memorised 'Article 21 is against the State' may accept Statement 1 without recalling the Vishaka exception. The Vishaka case is the primary counterexample that makes Statement 1 false.
solution.final_explanation:
The direct-versus-indirect horizontal application distinction is subtle but significant in Article 21 jurisprudence.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: While Article 21 is primarily a vertical right (enforceable against the State under Article 12), the Supreme Court has extended Article 21 obligations to private actors in specific contexts. Vishaka (1997) imposed binding sexual harassment guidelines on private employers — an indirect horizontal application. The MC Mehta absolute liability doctrine holds private industries liable for environmental harm affecting public Article 21 rights. The word 'never' makes Statement 1 categorically false.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) arose from the gang rape of a social worker. The Court held that workplace sexual harassment violates Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21, and issued comprehensive guidelines for prevention, prohibition, and redressal — binding on all employers, public and private, as a stop-gap measure until Parliament legislated. The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 gave these guidelines statutory form.

Value Addition:
• The concept of private bodies performing 'public functions' being treated as 'State' under Article 12 is a related but distinct doctrine.
• MC Mehta's 'absolute liability' (no exceptions available to enterprise) is stronger than common law 'strict liability' (Rylands v. Fletcher allows exceptions).
• Vishaka guidelines are the blueprint for the POSH (Prevention of Sexual Harassment) Act, 2013.

solution.concept_anchor: Hussainara Khatoon — undertrial detention beyond maximum sentence violates Article 21
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students may reason that bail is the conventional remedy for undertrial detention and assume courts would refer the matter to the trial court rather than directly intervene under Article 21.
elimination_logic: Identify the constitutional principle: prolonged undertrial detention beyond the maximum sentence for the alleged offence violates Article 21 — Hussainara Khatoon (1979).
Eliminate (c): The issue is constitutional (Article 21 violation), not merely procedural — the court can directly address it under Article 32/226 without restricting itself to procedural orders.
Eliminate (d): Referring back to the trial court for bail does not address the constitutional violation; the High Court has jurisdiction to release directly.
Eliminate (b): Article 20 protects against double jeopardy, ex post facto, and self-incrimination — not prolonged undertrial detention; the applicable provision is Article 21.
Select (a): Hussainara Khatoon established that Article 21 mandates release of undertrials who have been detained for longer than the maximum sentence for their alleged offence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) deploys plausible-fabrication by presenting a procedurally familiar remedy (referral to trial court for bail) as the appropriate constitutional response. Students who have studied regular bail jurisprudence but not the specific Hussainara Khatoon doctrine may select this option, not knowing that the constitutional court can directly order release as an Article 21 remedy without routing through the trial court.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario presents the core fact pattern of Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).

The applicable principle is that prolonged detention of an undertrial prisoner beyond the maximum period of imprisonment for the alleged offence is a per se violation of Article 21's right to personal liberty. Courts are constitutionally empowered to directly order release under these circumstances.

• Option (a) — Correct: Under the Hussainara Khatoon doctrine, when an undertrial has been detained beyond the maximum sentence for the alleged offence without trial, Article 21 is violated. The constitutional court (under Article 32 or 226) can directly order the prisoner's release as a constitutional remedy — not as a bail but as a fundamental rights remedy.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 20 protects against specific forms of arbitrary criminal process (ex post facto, double jeopardy, self-incrimination) but does not deal with trial delay or prolonged undertrial detention.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While procedural reform orders are valuable, Hussainara Khatoon established that the individual whose rights are being violated cannot be made to wait for systemic reform — immediate release is the remedy.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Referring back to the trial court reduces the constitutional remedy to a procedural one and does not directly address the Article 21 violation already established by the detention's duration.

Value Addition:
• Section 436A CrPC (now Section 479 BNSS) provides statutory backing: an undertrial who has served half the maximum sentence may be released on bail.
• Hussainara Khatoon led to the release of over 40,000 prisoners in Bihar alone.
• The right to speedy trial and the right to legal aid often arise together in undertrial cases — both derived from Article 21.

concepts_used: Article 21 and Capital Punishment

solution.concept_anchor: Death penalty — not per se unconstitutional; procedure must be just and fair
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who have studied the 'right to life' expansion under Article 21 and its dignity dimension may reason that capital punishment, being irreversible and a deprivation of life, must be unconstitutional under the expanded reading of Article 21.
elimination_logic: Recall Bachan Singh (1980): the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of death penalty — it is not per se unconstitutional under Article 21.
Eliminate (a): Bachan Singh explicitly held capital punishment is constitutional; 'per se unconstitutional' is wrong.
Eliminate (c): Machhi Singh (1983) established the five-category guidelines — not a blanket prohibition; the Court retained death penalty for qualifying cases.
Eliminate (d): Inordinate delay in execution is a violation of Article 21 (Shattrughan Chauhan, 2014) — but this is a distinct principle from whether death penalty itself is constitutional.
Confirm (b): Bachan Singh (1980) held death penalty constitutional but must be confined to 'rarest of rare' cases after following a procedure that is fair, just, and reasonable.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the expanded reading of Article 21 — students who know Article 21 now includes dignity, privacy, and humane treatment may logically extend this to argue capital punishment is unconstitutional. However, Bachan Singh (1980) directly addressed and rejected this argument: the 'procedure established by law' for capital punishment, if fair and just, satisfies Article 21. The trap is to apply the expansion without knowing the specific holding.
solution.final_explanation:
Capital punishment's constitutionality under Article 21 was definitively settled in Bachan Singh (1980).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) explicitly upheld the constitutional validity of the death penalty. It is not per se unconstitutional under Article 21 — as long as the procedure by which it is imposed is fair, just, and reasonable.
• Option (b) — Correct: Bachan Singh held that the death penalty is constitutional but must be confined to the 'rarest of rare' cases. The Court's reasoning was that the Maneka Gandhi procedural standard is satisfied when the trial procedure is fair, evidence is properly assessed, and the sentence is imposed by an independent judiciary with full opportunity of defence.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Machhi Singh (1983) provided guidelines for determining 'rarest of rare' but did not prohibit capital punishment — it operationalised its application.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While Shattrughan Chauhan (2014) held that delay in execution violates Article 21, this principle does not render the death penalty itself unconstitutional — it addresses the manner and timeliness of execution.

Value Addition:
• India retains the death penalty for specific IPC offences and special laws (POCSO, anti-terrorism statutes).
• 'Rarest of rare' — Machhi Singh categories: manner (brutal/diabolical), motive (pre-planned), anti-social character, magnitude (multiple victims), victim's personality.
• The Supreme Court is currently reviewing the consistency of 'rarest of rare' application across different benches — a live jurisprudential debate.

With reference to the constitutional validity of capital punishment in India, which of the following statements correctly reflects the position established by the Supreme Court?

(a) Capital punishment is per se unconstitutional under Article 21 because the expanded interpretation of the right to life includes the right to live with dignity, which is irreconcilable with the death penalty.
(b) Capital punishment is constitutionally valid under Article 21, provided it is imposed through a procedure that is fair, just, and reasonable, and is restricted to the 'rarest of rare' cases.
(c) Capital punishment has been prohibited by the Supreme Court through the 'rarest of rare' doctrine established in Machhi Singh (1983), which effectively made it inapplicable in practice.
(d) Capital punishment is constitutionally valid in general but automatically becomes unconstitutional under Article 21 if there is any delay in its execution after the mercy petition is decided.

Right to Know / Right to Information Under Article 21

solution.concept_anchor: RTI exceptions valid — right to know vs. right to privacy tension

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The exceptions to disclosure under the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Sections 8 and 9) are constitutionally valid restrictions on the judicially-evolved right to know, as fundamental rights — including those judicially derived from Article 21 — can be subject to reasonable limitations.
statement_analysis.reason: Even judicially-evolved fundamental rights derived from Article 21 can be restricted through fair, just, and reasonable procedure or through reasonable restrictions analogous to those applicable under Article 19(2). RTI Act exemptions are valid restrictions on the right to information, as confirmed by consistent judicial practice.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The right to privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017) and the right to information (S.P. Gupta, 1981) are both absolute rights derived from Article 21, and neither can be restricted even by legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Neither the right to privacy nor the right to information is absolute. Both are subject to restrictions — privacy through the three-fold test (legality, legitimate aim, proportionality), and the right to information through statutory exceptions like RTI Act Sections 8 and 9. No Article 21-derived right is absolute.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both rights are Article 21-derived may assume both statements present the same conclusion; Statement 2's error lies in the word 'absolute', which an inattentive student under time pressure may miss.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: RTI Act exemptions are widely accepted as valid restrictions on the right to know — correct.

Test Statement 2's 'absolute rights' qualifier: Puttaswamy (2017) explicitly laid down a three-fold restriction test for privacy — clearly not absolute; RTI has Sections 8/9 exceptions — clearly not absolute; Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the correct concept (both rights are Article 21-derived) with the false attribute (therefore both are absolute). Statement 2 conflates 'being a fundamental right' with 'being an absolute right' — a dangerous generalisation. No fundamental right in India is absolute; all can be restricted by fair procedure or reasonable restrictions. The three-fold Puttaswamy test and RTI's Sections 8/9 are the specific mechanisms of restriction.
solution.final_explanation:
Both the right to know and the right to privacy are Article 21-derived rights — but neither is absolute.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The RTI Act's exemptions in Sections 8 and 9 (covering national security, intelligence, cabinet deliberations, personal information, fiduciary relationships, etc.) are constitutionally valid limitations on the right to information. Even fundamental rights derived from Article 21 are not absolute and can be restricted by law that follows fair, just, and reasonable standards.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'absolute' is the error. K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) itself laid down a three-fold test — legality, legitimate aim, proportionality — precisely to govern when privacy can be restricted. The right to information is restricted by RTI Act Sections 8 and 9. Both rights coexist with restrictions; neither is beyond legislative or executive limitation.

Value Addition:
• The privacy-versus-RTI tension arises frequently: personal information exempted under Section 8(1)(j) of RTI Act is directly linked to the privacy right in Puttaswamy.
• Puttaswamy's proportionality standard is increasingly applied by courts to test whether laws restricting privacy are constitutionally valid.
• The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is the most significant post-Puttaswamy legislative response to the privacy fundamental right.
